description: ACL rule keys are a CLOSED set (PROTOCOL_SPEC §6.1, spec v1.27.0, #107). Loading a rule that carries any key outside `callers`, `targets`, `effect`, `description`, `conditions` MUST fail with ACLRuleError. A key nothing evaluates is otherwise dropped in silence, which widens an `allow` rule with no warning — the §6.1.1 defect class on the pattern side. `id`, `actions` and `priority` were reserved in earlier revisions and are evaluated by no implementation; they are rejected like any other unknown key, and an implementation SHOULD name them as reserved. Driver contract: build an ACL FILE containing `rule` under `rules:` with the given `default_effect`, load it through the SDK's file-loading entry point, and assert that loading succeeds when `expected_load` is "ok" and raises/returns an ACL rule error when it is "reject". Where the SDK exposes the message, assert it names the offending key.

test_cases.note: Control: the closed set itself must still load.
Both optional members of the closed set.

THE ESCALATION CASE. An operator writing `actions: ["describe"]` intends introspection only; before v1.27.0 the key was dropped and the rule granted execute on orders.* to every agent.* caller, with no warning. Being a schema-DECLARED property is why `additionalProperties: false` could not catch it — it is removed from the schema in the same change.
Reserved; note the schema documented it as having no effect on rule ordering, which first-match-wins already fixes.
A key from a proposal that has not landed. Silently dropping it would degrade the rule to a bare `allow` — which is why closing the set is a prerequisite for adding any new rule field.
`conditons` for `conditions`. Dropped silently before v1.27.0, so the rule granted unconditionally — the same shape as the misspelled-condition-key defect §6.1.2 closed, one level up.
A reserved key and an unrecognised one together; the message should account for both rather than stopping at the first.
